replies.author: cone-grill-dumping
replies.text:
magic-carpet-ride

Vanadium is not a fingerprint-resistant browser, Ironfox might have some fingerprint resistance but is not a complete anonymity solution. Tor Browser (as noted by the Graphene OS project) is the browser with the best fingerprint resistance, Graphene OS has also recommended Brave in the past but I recommend using it with a VPN to achieve anonymity.

In my experience it's best to have a browser where you do your everyday stuff and identify yourself (Vanadium is great for this), and one that hides your identity (like Brave + VPN, Mullvad Browser + VPN, or Tor Browser). Some people have also noted some success in using multiple browsers for different things, but given most Android browsers kinda suck for security or privacy I think two is a good number.

Note that Firefox browsers are less secure than Chromium and increase attack surface. Also that Brave, unlike Tor, does not hide your timezone or system language.

replies.author: mmmm
replies.text:
cone-grill-dumping recommend using it with a VPN to achieve anonymity.

That will not achieve anonymity. That will hide your IP from websites and prevent your ISP from seeing where you go. Good enough in most cases perhaps, but that's not anonymous. The only real way to achieve a modicum of anonymity is with Tor, and that's only with very careful use.

replies.author: cone-grill-dumping
replies.text:
mmmm

I would reread my post where I clearly pointed out that Graphene OS recommends Tor Browser for anonymity above all else. Brave is recommended if you're a VPN user.

I'm not a VPN user, so I didn't tell users how to get an anonymous VPN. What I did do is point to a resource that explains fingerprinting and tells users not to use JavaScript, as it increases fingerprinting risk. From my understanding, Tor Browser on safest, or Brave without scripts + an anonymous VPN are the two best options. I didn't say what is best for that user because it is not my threat model, and therefore not my place to sway their thinking. Tor is also not the only anonymity tool, and I try to avoid absolutes when advising others

Recommending a non-anonymous browser and one intended for anonymity is not insane advice. You wouldn't log into your bank on Tor Browser would ya?

That website is specifically recommending against using multiple browsers for clear web activities, which I agree with the website on. Every security researcher I've seen has recommended the use of an everyday browser alongside Tor Browser (for obvious reasons)

I already touched on how bad Firefox security is. Tor Browser is (unfortunately) the best attempt on any platform at fingerprint resistance (which was the entire point of this discussion). Ideally you'd run Tor Browser in a VM of some kind, like Whonix, to mitigate attack surface

replies.author: mmmm
replies.text: cone-grill-dumping The VPN inherently knows all. It can't possibly be anonymous. Sure you can use one for hiding your traffic from you ISP or who you are from the websites you visit, but nontheless, the VPN provider takes the role. You can trust them, that's fine. But you're in no way anonymous, even if you pay via anon means and do all the other trickery, and use a no logs VPN or whatever, it's not anonymous. Suggesting it is anonymous is definitely not good advice.

replies.author: cone-grill-dumping
replies.text:
Reboot

Whonix is really the best we have at the moment unfortunately, and the concept of sandboxing the Tor daemon in another VM is sound. If you're really concerned you can route any OS through the Whonix gateway for added anonymity

The Tor Browser bundle isn't really secure either, Whonix is a definitive step up from just running Tor Browser on bare metal. It's even a step up from running it in a VM, since Whonix leverages virtualization to ensure that if the Workstation is hacked your IP won't be leaked

replies.author: cone-grill-dumping
replies.text:
mmmm

We need to talk about threat model in relation to OP's situation, as they're looking to beat browser fingerprinting. IP is part of your fingerprint. I recommended ways to be anonymous to WEBSITES, which is what OP was looking for.

You're also bringing up trust and fingerprinting web traffic. You do realize exit relays can track your web traffic too right? You also have to trust Tor to not have their infrastructure compromised, which has happened. Tor is not a magic bullet, and we need to be able to recommend other options for users

replies.author: mmmm
replies.text:
cone-grill-dumping

Look, that's not the issue. The issue is this claim you made:

cone-grill-dumping Graphene OS has also recommended Brave in the past but I recommend using it with a VPN to achieve anonymity.

This is a dangerous claim because; no matter what extensions you add or how you pay for the VPN, or even what the VPN claims, this is not a path to any kind of anonymity. Yet you claim it is. You even recommend it. It is not the case though.

You're moving the goal posts.

I have stated already that Tor is not fool proof, mentioning several times it still needs care and attention. Regardless, it's the only way to achieve a modicum of anonymity. A VPN does no such thing, aside from protecting your IP from your ISP and your IP from websites visited. That's great if that's what one wants, many do - myself included. But it's not anonymous. You are not browsing the web anonymously, as in the meaning of the word anonymous.

replies.author: cone-grill-dumping
replies.text:
mmmm

I don't think that pointing out that I'm focusing on what OP needs and using layman language is moving the goal post.

Here's the definition of anonymous from Merriam Webster:

• of unknown authorship or origin

• not named or identified

• lacking individuality, distinction, or recognizability

There are VPNs out there that, under certain threat models, would serve to protect OP. We can presume OP is not a high value target, so the money, legal resources, or hacking expertise to deanonymize OP would probably be too great to put to use. Thus, OP remains anonymous -- paying with cash leaves no payment info, leaving no identifying information, leaving no name. If anything, Tor can harm certain threat models by making people stand out too much as compared to a VPN like Mullvad or I-VPN.

Tor is great because it requires no info to use and handles the browser fingerprinting threat, but it is highly fingerprintable to local network operators and guard nodes. Tor Browser is also insecure, which is why we're even needing this discussion.

Using the word anonymous was loaded, I'll admit. I have a bad habit of compromising correctness for being able to be understood by laymans. I don't think it was necessarily wrong, but loaded. I also feel that VPNs can be a useful tool to protect anonymity in some threat models, especially if you disable javascript and use a common browser. My mindset isn't that tools are inherently anonymous or private, but rather that they protect anonymity and privacy. Your choices online devalue your privacy and anonymity. However explaining that to OP in a post about browser fingerprinting felt like too much at the time

I'm open to having conversations about anonymizing technology and in what circumstances they work. We need other options than Tor, especially since no option is a true panacea

replies.author: mmmm
replies.text:
cone-grill-dumping I understood what you were getting at but yeah - loaded is a good way of saying it. I would have gone with "these tools can help with hiding your identity from certain parties when used correctly" rather than flat out and misleading 'anonymous'.

I also know what it means, no need for a cut and paste dictionary definition. The word anonymous, outside of its dictionary definition implies exactly that for anyone reading the word. People understand it as fully hiding onesself. It doesn't include half measures, and brave plus a VPN is exactly that.

It's all I'm trying to get across. Thanks for conceding a little though.
